name: Tear trough filler

lead: Tear trough filler uses hyaluronic acid injected under the eye to soften the hollow and shadow running from the inner corner of the eye across the cheek. People use it for a less tired, more rested look, quickly and with little downtime, and some treat it as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.

The gel adds volume along the tear trough groove, reducing the depth of the hollow and the shadow it casts. Published evidence includes a 100-patient case series, systematic reviews of technique and complications, and several registered trials of HA products for under-eye hollows. In forums it is discussed as a subtle correction, with users sharing cost and recovery impressions.

paras: A licensed clinician injects with either a needle or a blunt microcannula in an office visit, and a 2022 systematic review found no standardised preferred approach. People repeat treatments as the gel absorbs, and hyaluronidase can dissolve it.

Reviews describe side effects as generally mild and transient, such as swelling and bruising, though delayed complications can occur, and a case report described orbital compartment syndrome. Blindness from filler embolization is reported as rare but usually permanent. Fillers are regulated as medical devices.

angle.text: Tear trough filler softens the shadowed hollow under the eyes, giving a more rested look quickly and with little downtime. Hyaluronic acid is placed in the groove to reduce the hollow and its shadow. Some people treat it as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery, and a 100-patient case series and several registered trials exist.

lead: Tear trough filler is the injection of a dermal filler, usually hyaluronic acid (HA), into the tear trough, the groove or hollow that runs from the inner corner of the eye diagonally down across the lower eyelid and upper cheek. People have it to soften the shadowed hollow and the tired, dark-circled look that infraorbital hollows can give, which makes the eye area read as smoother and the midface as fuller; practitioners also describe it as a non-surgical alternative to lower eyelid surgery.[1][2][3][4]

The tear trough is regarded as a technically demanding area. A 2022 systematic review of HA technique found no standardized evidence-based approach to injecting filler there, whether with a hypodermic needle or a microcannula, and a separate systematic review of delayed complications reported that side effects are generally mild and transient but that delayed complications can occur.[2][3] The US Food and Drug Administration lists the periorbital area among areas it advises against injecting with dermal fillers, so under-eye treatment is generally an off-label use of products approved for other facial indications.[5]

Published evidence includes case series, systematic reviews of technique and complications, and registered trials of HA products for infra-orbital hollows.[1][2][3][6][7] In looksmaxxing forums, under-eye filler is discussed as a subtle correction with little visible change to the rest of the face, with users sharing cost and recovery impressions.[8]
infobox: Wikipedia gives about six months for most temporary wrinkle fillers; varies by product and person
FDA lists the periorbital area among areas it advises against injecting
Platelet-rich plasma, jawline and cheek filler, neuromodulators

paras: The tear trough, or nasojugal groove, is the depression below the lower eyelid, where the thin skin of the eyelid meets the cheek. Wikipedia's blepharoplasty article describes the tear trough as the transition from lower lid to cheek and notes that volume loss and fat herniation with age contribute to contour irregularities there.[9] Filler placed along it adds volume to reduce the hollow and the shadow it casts. A 2011 ophthalmic plastic surgery case series framed HA filler for the tear trough as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery.[1]

A 2024 review of periorbital rejuvenation describes dermal fillers as a way to camouflage orbital fat pseudoherniation and tear trough deformity, alongside neuromodulators that lift the brow and soften periorbital lines.[4] A review of the HA literature notes that, despite well-documented risks, injection in this area is not standardised, and compares needle and microcannula use.[3] A surgeon-reported series of 1,452 tear trough applications describes a three-point tangent technique that uses a blunt cannula to place filler along three lines tailored to each patient.[6]

sections.h: How people use it to improve their looks
paras: The appearance goal is a smoother transition from the lower eyelid to the cheek, less visible shadowing and a more rested look. Because the dark under-eye hollow is partly a shadow effect of the groove, adding volume can change how light falls on the area without changing the skin itself.[4][9] Users describe the result as a small correction that is noticeable in person without making the face look overdone.[8]

Treatment is usually a short office visit with little scheduled downtime. One looksmax.org poster reported only some swelling and almost no downtime, and said the change was easier to see in person than in photographs.[8] A retrospective review of 447 patients who had 706 infraorbital HA filler treatments found swelling in over half of the patients not given a swelling-reducing additive, and the amount of swelling correlated with the volume injected.[10]

Alongside tear trough filler, people discuss cheek and midface filler, which supports the area from below, as well as skin treatments for under-eye pigmentation and, for more advanced lower lid changes, surgery such as transconjunctival blepharoplasty with fat repositioning.[9]

Hyaluronic acid is among the most common filler materials because it occurs naturally in vertebrates and is biocompatible and biodegradable, and manufacturers usually cross-link it, often with BDDE, so that it lasts longer in tissue.[11] Wikipedia's article on hyaluronic acid describes HA as a gel that smooths facial wrinkles and lasts roughly six to twelve months, and notes that enzymes called hyaluronidases degrade HA.[12] Wikipedia states that most wrinkle fillers are temporary, lasting about six months, with duration varying by skin health, provider skill, filler type and the activity level of the treated area.[11]

Studies of tear trough filler typically specify the product. The 2011 case series used a stabilized HA gel marketed as Perlane, and a registered randomized study evaluated RHA Redensity Eye against no treatment in people with infra-orbital hollows.[1][7] Wikipedia notes that Galderma's Restylane range may be used for orbital troughs, under and around the eyes.[13] The delayed-complications review also counted poly-L-lactic acid and calcium hydroxyapatite among products reported in tear trough cases, though HA was the most commonly reported.[2]

The systematic review of HA techniques compared hypodermic needle with microcannula delivery. It found 42 eligible articles (20 using needles, 12 using cannulas and 10 on adverse events), with most graded as Level III retrospective descriptive studies, and concluded that no standardized, evidence-based approach exists for the area.[3] A series of 1,452 applications to the orbits of 583 patients by one surgeon, treated between 2016 and 2020, described a three-point tangent technique, offered as a practical way to approach the hollow.[6]

A retrospective review of 706 treatments by a single injector looked at low-dose triamcinolone mixed with HA filler as a way to reduce post-injection swelling under the eyes: swelling occurred in 51 percent of those without the additive and 23 percent of those with it, and the incidence of swelling rose with the amount of filler injected.[10]

A review chapter on periorbital rejuvenation places filler among the options for the lower eyelid region.[4] The delayed-complications review draws on published cases to catalogue when problems appear after the first weeks.[2]

Lower blepharoplasty is the surgical counterpart. Wikipedia describes a transcutaneous approach through an incision below the lashes, used when skin laxity is significant, and a transconjunctival approach through the inner eyelid surface that leaves no external scar, as well as fat repositioning, in which orbital fat is redistributed along the infraorbital rim to smooth the lid-cheek transition.[9] Surgery is usually an outpatient procedure of one to three hours, with swelling and bruising that generally resolve over several weeks.[9]
Biological approaches have also been registered for study, including platelet-rich fibrin for tear trough rejuvenation and platelet-rich plasma for the nasojugal fold.[14][15]

In the US the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices, and a provider prescribes and performs the injection; in the UK and EEA they are non-prescription devices needing a CE mark, which does not require proof of medical efficacy.[11] Wikipedia reports more than 140 fillers on the UK and European market against only six approved in the US.[11]

The FDA's consumer page on dermal fillers says that absorbable fillers are approved for wrinkles and folds and for augmenting areas such as the lips, cheeks, chin and back of the hand in adults 22 and older, and it lists the periorbital area among areas where it advises against injection. The agency also advises against buying fillers online or injecting them oneself, because products may be counterfeit or unapproved.[5]

A consecutive interventional case series reported one surgeon's 18-month experience with HA gel (Perlane) as a tear trough filler: 198 eyes of 100 patients, mostly female (87 percent) and white (89 percent), with a mean follow-up of 5.1 months and an assessment that included masked grading of photographs and a satisfaction survey.[1]

Systematic reviews have examined delayed complications after tear trough filler and the HA techniques used. The delayed-complications review analysed 52 cases from 28 articles, 98 percent of them female with an average age of 48.3 years, and reported swelling as the most common delayed complication followed by lumps or nodules.[2][3] The 1,452-application series and the 706-treatment triamcinolone review are retrospective single-injector reports.[6][10]

Registered trials include a randomized comparison of an HA filler (RHA Redensity Eye) versus no treatment for infra-orbital hollows, tear trough deformity and wrinkles (NCT04577898, 248 participants, completed), a pilot phase 4 study combining two HA fillers for lower-eyelid rejuvenation (NCT00852241, 18 participants), an 11-participant prospective evaluation of infraorbital filler (NCT05694286), and a 73-participant satisfaction study of periorbital Juvéderm fillers with botulinum toxin (NCT05647551).[7][16][17][18]

Alternative biological approaches are also registered, including platelet-rich fibrin for tear trough rejuvenation (NCT03313934, 10 participants, status unknown) and a platelet-rich plasma study for the nasojugal fold that was withdrawn before enrolling participants (NCT03255681).[14][15]

A systematic review of delayed complications after tear trough filler reported that side effects are generally mild and transient but that delayed complications may occur, including swelling, lumps or nodules and xanthelasma-like reactions, and set out to catalogue them from the published literature.[2] A case report described the first reported orbital compartment syndrome after tear trough filler injection: a retrobulbar haemorrhage managed with an emergency lateral canthotomy and cantholysis, with no lasting visual compromise, and the authors called for greater awareness among injectors.[19]

Wikipedia lists common filler effects such as bruising, redness, pain and itching, rarer infection and allergic reactions, and rare but usually permanent blindness from retrograde embolization into the ophthalmic and retinal arteries.[11]

Wikipedia states that embolic complications of filler are more frequent with autologous fat, followed by HA, and that vascular events can also cause delayed skin necrosis.[11] The FDA names unintended injection into a blood vessel as the most serious risk and says its consequences, which can include tissue death, vision abnormalities including blindness and stroke, can be serious and may be permanent; it advises people to seek immediate care for unusual pain, vision changes or skin discoloration after injection.[5] Wikipedia notes that hyaluronidase enzymes degrade HA, the basis on which clinicians reverse HA filler in some complications.[12]

Google Trends analyses have examined public interest in cosmetic facial procedures during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and fluctuations in searches for cosmetic procedures.[20][21] These analyses address general interest rather than tear trough filler outcomes.

On looksmax.org, one user posted about having tear trough and jaw filler, describing it as giving small corrections that are immediately noticeable in person without looking artificial, with only some swelling and little downtime, and reporting a total cost of about 450 US dollars from a plastic surgeon with strong reviews. The poster added that the difference was hard to capture in photographs.[8] The original poster offered to answer questions about the procedure.[8]

Under-eye filler sits in forum discussion with other "softmaxxing" and hardmaxxing options for the eye area, such as blepharoplasty and cheek or midface support, as a lower-commitment route that can be reversed in the case of HA products.[9][12]

lore.intro: Tear trough filler is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-downtime way to correct under-eye hollows alongside other facial fillers.[8]

claims.claim: Tear trough filler gives a noticeable correction without looking plastic
Filler is a non-surgical alternative to lower eyelid surgery
Cannula injection is safer than needle injection
HA filler can be undone if the result is not wanted
Swelling after under-eye filler can be reduced
The under-eye area carries serious but rare risks

timeline.event: Karl Meyer and John Palmer first isolate hyaluronic acid, the substance later used in most tear trough fillers, from bovine vitreous.[12]
A pilot phase 4 study of two combined HA fillers for lower-eyelid rejuvenation begins (NCT00852241).[16]
Case series of HA filler for tear trough rejuvenation as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery published.[1]
Start of the treatment period (2016 to 2020) reported in the 1,452-application cannula series.[6]
Randomized study of RHA Redensity Eye versus no treatment for infra-orbital hollows begins (NCT04577898).[7]
Systematic reviews of delayed complications and of HA injection techniques for the tear trough published; a review reports triamcinolone mixed with HA reduces swelling.[2][3][10]
Series of 1,452 tear trough applications describing the three-point tangent technique published.[6]
Case report of orbital compartment syndrome after tear trough filler and a periorbital rejuvenation review published.[19][4]
